origin: Original workshop built by Muse (AI assistant) on 19 November 2026 at Steven Powell's direction, from his own framing in the Everyday Cool ideas side chat that evening. Of the four queued STEM rooms he ordered saved that night (Math, Engineering, Earth, Computing — 'save that list I want to do them all'), Engineering went first, Math second, Earth third; Computing is fourth and last, on his tap of the option card: 'Build Everyday Computing — finish the four.' His framing, built to here: binary and gates — counting in twos, AND/OR/XOR made playable, pattern recognition on top — tying straight into his troubleshooting aphorism (most people work problems by rules and logic gates, like a map; the real skill is pattern recognisers seeing similarities across gates, and the inference 'something here might apply there' is 'the real vudu'), which hangs as a panel in Nerd Heaven with the gates-pattern infographic. Three additions arrived from Steven mid-build and are folded in: a free-form logic builder (place AND, OR, NOT, XOR — NAND and NOR too — wire outputs into inputs, watch lamps evaluate live; anchor #logic-builder; its circuit model is tested, including an XOR assembled from AND/OR/NOT across all input cases and a self-wired gate honestly reported unsettled); the infographic itself, copied byte-for-byte from the Nerd Heaven room as a room asset with its AI-generated disclosure — and with the known flaw recorded rather than repaired: the image's own explainer text gets its gate logic wrong (an XOR shown lighting on 1 and 1, a NOT that does not flip), errors Steven was told about and chose to publish as-is, so the page names them and holds its benches to the opposite standard, correct and tested; and a link from Nerd Heaven's aphorism panel to the builder, recorded in that room's COLLECTION.md local-changes list. The room: the binary bench (eight switches, 0–255, both directions), the gates bench (six gates, truth tables that highlight the row being played), the half adder (XOR sum, AND carry, all four cases), the toy net (three gates recognising 1-0-1 out of eight patterns, near misses counted), the logic builder, the sizes bench (the decimal and binary ladders kept apart — a kibibyte is 8192 bits, a kilobyte 8000), the sorting bench (bubble sort, narrated), the tea test for algorithms, and seven verified links out. It enters the catalog under 'Science' with hubParent 'stem-room', immediately after Everyday Earth, as the twenty-ninth entry and the STEM Room's tenth workshop. This folder is the maintained original. Web-first, per Steven's plan set the same evening: the four queue rooms go live on the web one at a time and reach the desktop app together in a single later release — with this room live, all four are up.
